Author: @christopherlenahan3906
Content: To grind AlO2 you need a hardness of 61HRC minimum(Mohs 9)..Carbon-Steel has a limit of 70HRC, so those rolls are a wear item.. Replacing those precision ground rolls on a less than once a year would be quite the expense. I would recommend he test tungsten-carbide coating a set of used rolls. I have seen amazing reduction in wear with that on potassium-salt slurry parts. Although not an issue of pressure, certainly a wear issue.

Author: @JaroslavDohnal
Content: The SEM actually has a 3-stage vacuum system. Turbomolecular pumps will get you to about 10E-5 Pa, the shottky emitter (the actual source of the electron beam) needs to be operated at 10E-8 Pa at least. Thats what you see with the read and silver (gamma vacuum) boxes, those are getter and ion pumps, using constants stream of some material (usually titanium for its reactivity) to basically catch and stick the air atoms in this stream of matter to the pump wall. Getting to high vacuums is quite interesting. I work for Tescan, it's nice to see the machines used in real applications. In semiconductor manufacturing they usually use cryopumps as a third stage pump, they are lot mor expensive, but much cleaner.

Author: @EkiToji
Content:
Since Steve seemed interested in vacuum pumps, the reason you need a second stage for high vacuum (so low pressure) is all based on mean-free path.  That just means on average how far a particle goes before colliding with something.  At low vacuum you can just use a pretty standard pump because air is a fluid and we call it a roughing pump.  At some point though you start having to treat the remaining air as individual particles and so diffusion instead of fluid mechanics dominate and that requires a completely different pump structure.  Plus even your basic vacuum lubricants will start to evaporate at some low vapor pressure and that limits how high of vacuum you can go while also potentially contaminating your sample.

A turbo pump is literally just multiple layers of fan blades spinning typically around 40k-50k RPM so that any particle a blade hits will get deflected downwards and away from the vacuum chamber.  Multiple stages of those blades just helps to create an overall useful pressure differential across the entire pump and prevent molecules from escaping back into the chamber.  There are other types like a diffusion pump that shoots oil vapor out and downward to do the same thing or a cryopump that relies on trapping some gasses by condensing them onto a surface chilled typically by helium so you can get very cold.  A lot of times you can even combine these such as having a nice cold surface cooled by liquid nitrogen that acts as a cryotrap by reducing the kinetic energy of molecules so they hang out down near a diffusion pump for longer and are more likely get to get pushed out.

In any case though a high vacuum pump doesn't work under low vacuums and more importantly can only handle a relatively slight pressure differential across the pump.  So behind that high vacuum pump you'll have a backing pump that can push those molecules out into atmosphere.  Usually that is just your same roughing pump and you just use a valve so the roughing pump stops getting exposed to the chamber pressure but instead to the back end of the high vacuum pump.

Why all this is necessary is for electron microscopes goes right back to mean-free path but this time for electrons.  You need sufficiently high vacuum so the electrons hit your sample instead of air molecules, and the same for electrons emitted from the sample to get to the detector.

Content: In my experience, to prevent the flickering when filming screens with a camera it's helpful to set the shutter speed of the camera to 100 (for 60fps) or 50 (for 30fps) when filming in a region with a 50Hz power grid (e.g. Europe). The shutter speed does not have to be exactly twice the framerate (although some cameras only allow for that ratio and caused the myth that only filming in 25/50fps in regions with a 50Hz power grid is the solution), but it should be a multiple of the power grids Hz. If someone else has had a different experience with that, please let me know.

Content:
My only issue, is that the video wasn't longer!   I'd have loved to hear Roman explain more stuff to steve, and go into  more detail.  But I'm sure Steve didn't want a 3 hour long video ( I'd watch that ). 

A lot of this stuff is super easy to understand, but it's super rare to actually get to see it, and be explained by someone so open to sharing information.  

On a side note for Americans.........This is why supply chains, and good relations with other nations is a good thing.  Roman imports a lot of the base materials from other countries.  He then put's them all together into a product to sell.  If germany decided to suddenly fuck over their trading partners, Roman wouldn't be able to get the materials he needs, or he'd have to pay a much higher price to get them from a different country, that isn't as efficient at extracting the materials, or processing them to be as pure as he needs, or have the correct size distribution.  If Thermal Grizzly's operation was in America right now,  He'd be totally fucked, with the import taxes, and the rare earth shipment stoppage china put on the USA.

Author: @gabiballetje
Content:
Why is thermal paste so expensive ? you take a certain amount of some things and mix them together and voila, and it's just gunk, you end up with a paste, why is it so much ?
Well...
Ingredients, expensive, they need to be good, right amount, right size, you have to check that with a very expensive machine and someone able to run it.
When mixing, the right stuff again, right amount, in a certain mnachine with the right "air" and right amount of moisture in the air, for that you need to buy barrels of this substance, it's annoying to work, then you have an expensive mixing machine also maintaining the right moisture, temperature, blades, grind it all, take out the air, and it takes about a day.
And then you have one pot.
And then you have to transport and fill small syringes with the right amount, because going over 5% on every syringe will cost you a lot in the long run.
And the better you want this stuff to be the worse everything gets, more time and effort and machine and materials it takes.
Making a single pot takes two days, and during that time the machines run, costing power, machines aren't cheap, and you pay for people to do and check all of this, and they are NOT making minimum wage, adn then everything needs to be cleaned no doubt, and if a part of a machine breaks, well, need a new part, and they're probably not cheap either.
Sooo... yeah, expensive. For a good reason.
So, go try and make the same or better stuff at home XD
So, you want the "best" stuff or not. Best depending on exactly what you want.
If you don't have to apply it regularly, and buy a hundreds of dollars costing CPU, GPU, Mobo, PSU, fans, case, why complain about a few tubes or paste that cost a fraction of your build.
